title: Ising-machine-like Driving Condition Restrictions in SSBM and Additional Pseudo-annealing- Driving Method for SSBM that Achieves Best Cut Value Search -
abstract: In our previous paper, we described the proposal and validation of a new physical implementation-type simulator (spontaneous symmetry breaking machine (SSBM)) for a combinatorial optimization problem that utilizes a phenomenon dual to the model in which a pseudo-spin many-body system is created by spontaneous symmetry breaking. Furthermore, we performed numerical simulations with different initial fluctuations on a large-scale benchmark problem (K_{2000}) and reported that we identified a condition under which pseudo-spin patterns gradually converge during the solution search process to ultimately form a single pattern and that the cut value of this converged solution reached 99.7% of the known best. In this paper, we discuss the conditions under which the SSBM can exhibit behavior analogous to that of a continuous-variable-type Ising machine, and report that by adding an effect similar to physical annealing to these conditions, the SSBM can be made to search for the best known cuts in K_{2000}.
summary: The paper improves a specialized simulator called the SSBM for solving combinatorial optimization problems. It achieves this by modifying the machine's driving conditions to mimic continuous-variable Ising machines and by incorporating a pseudo-annealing effect. These modifications allow the physical simulator to search more effectively, reaching near state-of-the-art solutions.
main_problem: Developing a high-performance solver for complex combinatorial optimization problems, such as finding the best cut value for K2000.
main_result: By restricting driving conditions and adding a pseudo-annealing effect to the SSBM, the system can achieve search performance comparable to known state-of-the-art methods, approaching the best known cut values.
method: The authors analyze the dynamics of the Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking Machine (SSBM) by imposing specific driving condition restrictions and introducing a pseudo-annealing term into its discrete evolution equations.
model_or_system: The core system is the SSBM, a physical simulator based on spontaneous symmetry breaking phenomena using dissipative elements. Its dynamics are governed by an iteration equation ($\phi_{i+m} = \sin^2(\gamma^2 \phi_i + 	heta_B)$) and pseudo-spin interactions.
key_observables: The primary observable is the 'cut value' achieved during the solution search process, alongside the evolution and histogram of pseudo-spin patterns ($\phi_i$).
important_parameters: Nesting number (restricted to 12), noise intensity schedule for annealing, and coupling parameters ($\gamma, 	heta_B$).
main_assumptions: The SSBM is treated as a discrete system, requiring the introduction of a *pseudo*-annealing effect to mimic continuous-variable techniques like those involving Nosé–Hoover methods.
figures_summary: Figures compare SSBM behavior under simple restrictions (Point 1) versus when pseudo-annealing (Point 2) is added. The histograms show that adding annealing shifts the cut value distribution toward higher, better values.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the baseline performance of SSBM; it then discusses imposing quasi-static restrictions analogous to continuous IMs; finally, it introduces and validates the addition of a pseudo-annealing effect to further enhance search capability.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses how non-equilibrium dynamics (like those in dissipative physical simulators) can be tuned using concepts borrowed from thermal physics (annealing) to solve hard optimization problems, which is highly relevant for quantum computation and complex system modeling.
